Below are several proven strategies that an apartment building can pursue to lower its heating costs. Depending on the building’s age, construction and existing systems, you may choose a combination of measures for greatest effect.

1. Improve the building envelope  
   • Wall insulation – add or upgrade cavity-wall or external‐wall insulation to reduce heat loss.  
   • Roof and attic insulation – ensure lofts and flat roofs are well insulated with the recommended U-values.  
   • Floor insulation – insulate suspended ground floors or slab edges where feasible.  
   • High-performance windows and doors – replace single‐glazed units with double- or triple-glazed, low-emissivity frames.

2. Upgrade the heating plant and distribution  
   • Modern condensing or low-temperature boilers – these extract more heat from the same fuel or district-heating supply.  
   • Heat pumps (air-source or ground-source) – can replace or supplement existing boilers, especially in well-insulated buildings.  
   • Hydronic panel/radiator retrofits – install thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) and balance the system hydraulically so each apartment can control its own temperature.

3. Install or optimize ventilation with heat recovery  
   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – recovers up to 80–90% of the heat from outgoing stale air.  
   • Demand-controlled ventilation – uses CO₂ or humidity sensors to supply fresh air only when needed, reducing heat loss.

4. Implement smart controls and building automation  
   • Weather-compensated control – adjusts flow temperatures in response to outside temperature, avoiding overheating.  
   • Time- and zone-based thermostats – allow apartments or corridors to have tailored schedules and set-back temperatures.  
   • Remote monitoring and fault detection – identifies system inefficiencies or malfunctions (e.g., pump failures, boiler drift).

5. Optimize maintenance and operation  
   • Regular servicing of boilers, pumps and valves – keeps plant running at peak efficiency.  
   • Flushing and balancing of heating circuits – removes sludge in radiators and ensures even heat distribution.  
   • Resident awareness campaigns – promote simple behaviors (e.g., closing windows when heating is on, keeping vents free).

6. Consider renewable or alternative energy sources  
   • Solar thermal collectors – pre-heat domestic hot water and reduce load on central heating.  
   • Photovoltaic panels – generate electricity on-site, which can offset the building’s electricity-driven heating pumps or ventilation fans.  
   • Biofuel or wood-pellet boilers – an option where biomass is locally available and sustainably sourced.

7. Financial incentives and planning  
   • Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) recommendations – follow the improvement measures listed in the EPC to target the most cost-effective upgrades.  
   • Government grants or low-interest loans – many programmes exist to subsidize insulation, renewable installations or system upgrades.  
   • Phased renovation plan – tackle the most impactful items first (e.g., roofs and walls) and spread investment over several years.

By combining envelope improvements, system upgrades, smart controls and ongoing maintenance—and by taking advantage of subsidies and EPC guidance—an apartment building can significantly reduce its heating costs while improving comfort and lowering its carbon footprint.

An energy declaration (energideklaration) is a comprehensive report that helps a building board understand the current energy performance of their property and identify cost-effective improvement measures. It typically includes:

• Energy class and rating  
  – A letter grade (A–G) summarizing the building’s overall energy performance (epc_egienergiklass).  
  – If multiple assessments exist, the latest rating is the valid one.

• Annual energy use  
  – Total energy consumption expressed in kWh per m² heated floor area (Atemp) and in kWh per year.  
  – Breakdown by energy carriers (e.g. district heating, electricity, oil).

• Building characteristics  
  – Heated floor area (Atemp) in m² (epc_egenatemp).  
  – Number of above-ground floors (epc_egenantalplan) and stairwells (epc_egenantaltrapphus).  
  – Building type (apartment block, detached house, etc.; epc_egenbyggnadstyp).  
  – Owner-built flag (epc_egennybyggar), if applicable.

• Primary energy demand and CO₂ emissions  
  – Estimates of the building’s primary energy use including losses.  
  – Associated greenhouse gas emissions.

• Recommended energy-saving measures  
  – A prioritized list of retrofit or behavioural measures (e.g. improved insulation, window upgrades, optimized ventilation, boiler or heat-pump replacement).  
  – Estimated energy savings, investment costs and payback times for each measure.

Why it’s useful for a building board  
– Provides a clear baseline of current energy performance and running costs.  
– Helps to budget and plan maintenance or renovation projects.  
– Supports decision-making on which upgrades deliver the greatest energy and cost savings.  
– Can be used to meet regulatory requirements and to communicate sustainability goals to residents or stakeholders.

To lower your building’s heating costs most effectively, you should focus first on reducing heat losses through the building envelope and then on upgrading the heating system and controls. Even without specific EPC data on your property, the following prioritized measures are generally the most cost-effective:

1. Improve insulation and airtightness  
   • Add or upgrade insulation in the attic, walls and basement/slab-on-ground.  
   • Seal gaps around windows, doors, service penetrations and in junctions between building elements.  

2. Upgrade glazing and window frames  
   • Replace single- or poorly insulated double-glazing with modern low-E, gas-filled units.  
   • Choose well-insulated frames and ensure correct installation to avoid thermal bridges.  

3. Install or optimize ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR)  
   • A balanced mechanical system with heat recovery can recapture 60–90 % of the heat in outgoing air.  
   • Properly sized ductwork and regular filter maintenance are key to good performance.  

4. Modernize the heating system  
   • Replace an old boiler with a high-efficiency condensing boiler or, better yet, a ground- or air-source heat pump.  
   • Size the system correctly to match your actual heating demand (Atemp) rather than oversizing “just in case.”  

5. Improve controls and distribution  
   • Fit thermostatic radiator valves or smart zone controls so you only heat the rooms you need, when you need them.  
   • Use weather-compensated or outdoor-reset controls to avoid overheating on mild days.  

6. Maintain and monitor  
   • Have your heating system serviced annually to keep efficiency high.  
   • Monitor energy use (e.g. via sub-meters or a smart metering system) to track savings and detect faults early.  

By tackling the building envelope first (insulation, airtightness, windows, ventilation recovery) you reduce the amount of heat you need. Only then does it make sense to invest in new heat-generating equipment, since you’ll need a smaller, more efficient system once losses are cut. This sequence also tends to give the best return on investment and a more comfortable indoor climate.

4. Renewable energy and carbon reduction  
   • Evaluate on-site renewables: solar PV on rooftops, solar thermal for hot water, or geothermal heat pumps.  
   • Consider procuring green electricity or carbon offset schemes if on-site generation is limited.

5. Operational efficiency and maintenance  
   • Implement a building-management system (BMS) to monitor energy, temperature, humidity and air flows in real time.  
   • Plan preventive maintenance on major systems to extend asset life and avoid unplanned downtime.

6. User engagement and behaviour  
   • Educate occupants on energy-saving habits (e.g. temperature set-backs, switching off lights and equipment).

Direct-acting (also called “instant” or “direct-acting”) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use, but that does not mean they are the most energy-efficient choice overall. Here’s why:

1. Point-of-use efficiency versus primary energy  
   • Point-of-use: Electric resistive heaters are nearly 100 percent efficient in turning electricity into heat.  
   • Primary energy: If the electricity comes from fossil-fuel–based generation, the overall efficiency from fuel extraction to your radiator can be 30–40 percent (and even lower in some grids). Renewables improve this picture, but generation and transmission losses still apply.

2. Operating costs  
   • Electricity price: In most markets, electricity is one of the more expensive heating fuels (measured cost per kWh of delivered heat).  
   • Tariffs: Unless you have access to off-peak or specially contracted rates, running direct electric heating can be costly over a heating season.

3. Control and comfort  
   • Fast response: Direct-acting radiators heat up and cool down quickly, allowing precise room‐by‐room control.  
   • Zoning: You can switch off radiators in unused rooms, which can save energy in a well-insulated building.

4. Comparison with alternatives  
   • Heat pumps (air-source or ground-source) typically deliver 3–5 kWh of heat for each kWh of electricity consumed (Coefficient of Performance, COP = 3–5). This makes them 200–400 percent more efficient in terms of primary energy.  
   • Biofuel or district heating systems may also offer lower running costs, depending on your local energy mix and infrastructure.

5. When direct electric radiators can make sense  
   • Supplementary or occasional heating (e.g., in a seldom-used guest room or bathroom).  
   • Very well-insulated buildings with low overall heat demand.  
   • Where installation of a larger heating system (boiler or heat pump) is impractical or prohibitively expensive.

Conclusion  
While direct-acting electric radiators deliver heat with 100 percent point-of-use efficiency and offer excellent responsiveness, they are generally more expensive to run and have a higher primary-energy footprint than heat pumps or modern district/biofuel heating. They are best employed as supplemental or zoned heaters rather than as a sole source of space heating in cold climates.

Here are several practical steps you can take to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators, both in terms of comfort and energy efficiency:

1. Fit and use individual thermostatic controls  
   • Install a thermostat (or thermostatic radiator valve) on each unit so you can set different temperatures for different rooms.  
   • Aim for around 20 °C in living areas, 17–18 °C in bedrooms and 16 °C in seldom-used spaces.

2. Program timers or use a smart control system  
   • Schedule the radiators to switch on just before you wake up and switch off shortly after you leave home.  
   • Use setback periods overnight (drop temperature by 2–3 °C) and during work hours to reduce consumption.

3. Zone your heating  
   • Group radiators into zones (e.g. living/dining, bedrooms, bathrooms) so you only heat the areas in use.  
   • Close valves completely in unused rooms.

4. Take advantage of off-peak electricity tariffs  
   • If your supplier offers “night-store” or Economy 7/10 tariffs, run your radiators at lower power during peak-rate hours and at higher power when electricity is cheaper.  
   • Program overnight charging to top up the heat store and then trickle-feed during the day.

5. Maintain clear airflow around the radiator  
   • Avoid placing furniture, curtains or drying clothes directly in front of the panel.  
   • Allow at least 10 cm of clearance above and 5 cm at the sides so convected air can circulate.

6. Fit reflective foil behind radiators on external walls  
   • A thin reflective barrier between the radiator and the wall will bounce more heat back into the room instead of letting it be absorbed by the masonry.

7. Bleed radiators regularly  
   • Air pockets reduce output. Bleed units once or twice a season to ensure the entire panel heats up evenly.

8. Improve your building’s thermal envelope  
   • Good insulation in walls, loft and underfloor will reduce the heat demand.  
   • Draught-proof windows and doors to minimise losses from infiltration.

9. Use “frost-protection” mode when away  
   • If you’re on holiday or the property is unoccupied for several days, set radiators to a low frost-guard level (e.g. 5–7 °C) rather than switching them off entirely. This prevents cold-weather damage and avoids the higher power surge required to re-heat a cold room.

10. Monitor and refine  
   • Keep an eye on your electricity consumption and indoor comfort.  
   • Adjust set-points and schedules gradually to find the right balance between comfort and cost.

By combining precise control, smart scheduling, basic maintenance and improved insulation, you can optimize both the performance and the running cost of direct-acting electric radiators.

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water (DHW) systems can both lower operating costs and reduce environmental impact. Here are the main strategies:

1. Insulate Storage and Distribution  
   • Tank insulation: Fit or upgrade a high-performance jacket (at least 75 mm of foam) around your hot-water cylinder to minimize standby losses.  
   • Pipework insulation: Insulate all hot-water pipes (and cold-water feed to nearby taps) with at least 13 mm of closed-cell foam to reduce heat losses and improve delivery temperature.  

2. Optimize Temperature Settings  
   • Lower thermostat set-point: Reducing the cylinder thermostat from, say, 60 °C to 55 °C can cut heat losses by up to 10 % while still controlling legionella risk.  
   • Use thermostatic mixing valves: These allow maintaining a higher storage temperature (for safety) but deliver water at a comfortable lower temperature to taps, preventing scalding and minimising overheating.

3. Deploy High-Efficiency Generation Technologies  
   • Heat-pump water heaters: Air-source or ground-source heat pumps can produce DHW with coefficients of performance (COPs) of 3–4, meaning they deliver 3–4 kWh of heat for every kWh of electricity consumed.  
   • Condensing boilers: Choose a boiler with a dedicated DHW mode and high modulation ratio. Condensing operation during light DHW draws further improves efficiency.  

4. Incorporate Renewable Heat Sources  
   • Solar thermal collectors: A properly sized solar-thermal array (flat-plate or evacuated tube) can cover 30–70 % of annual DHW demand in temperate climates.  
   • Photovoltaic-driven booster: Pair PV panels with an electric heat-pump or resistive element—ideally via an intelligent controller or diverter—to use surplus solar electricity for water heating.

5. Install On-Demand or Point-Of-Use Systems  
   • Instantaneous (tankless) water heaters: Reduce storage losses by generating hot water only when needed. These systems must be sized correctly and may require higher electrical or gas supply capacity.  
   • Local boosters: Small point-of-use units under sinks eliminate long pipe runs and wasted water while maintaining temperature.

6. Recover and Re-Use Waste Heat  
   • Drain-water heat recovery: Install a plate-type heat exchanger in the drain stack below showers to pre-heat incoming cold water by capturing heat from warm wastewater, typically recovering 20–30 % of shower energy.  
   • Combined systems: Some heat pumps and boilers offer integrated wastewater or flue-gas recovery options.

7. Control and Scheduling  
   • Time-of-use control: Program DHW heating to operate during off-peak electricity or gas-tariff hours.  
   • Weather- or load-compensation: Advanced controllers adjust water-heating temperatures and charging times based on outdoor conditions and occupancy patterns.

8. Perform Regular Maintenance  
   • Descale and flush: Hard-water deposits reduce heat‐transfer efficiency. Annual flushing or use of a softener/mineral filter helps maintain performance.  
   • Check insulation integrity and thermostat calibration.  
   • Service burners, heat-pump refrigerant levels and circulation pumps to ensure design performance is sustained.

By combining good insulation, efficient generation, smart controls and, where feasible, renewable sources or heat recovery, domestic hot-water systems can routinely achieve energy savings of 20–50 % compared to conventional, uninsulated storage boiler setups.

Optimizing domestic hot‐water (DHW) production in a multi‐unit residential building involves improving both the generation efficiency and the distribution system. Below are several strategies—grouped by system component—that you can consider:

1. Heat Generation  
   • High‐Efficiency Boilers or Heat Pumps  
     – Replace old boilers with modern condensing types that recover latent heat from flue gases.  
     – Consider electric or gas‐fired heat pumps dedicated to DHW; they can achieve COPs (coefficients of performance) of 3–4.  
   • Solar Thermal Integration  
     – Install roof‐mounted solar collectors to preheat storage tanks. Even in Sweden’s climate, solar preheating can cover 20–40 % of annual DHW needs.  
   • Wastewater Heat Recovery  
     – Fit a plate‐heat exchanger in the drain line to recover energy from shower and sink wastewater and use it to preheat incoming cold water.

2. Storage and Buffering  
   • Appropriately Sized Storage Tanks  
     – Avoid oversized tanks (excess heat losses) and undersized tanks (peak‐demand shortages).  
     – Use stratified tanks or twin‐coil tanks to separate solar and boiler circuits for better layering of temperatures.  
   • Insulation  
     – Insulate all storage vessels and exposed pipework with at least 50 mm of closed‐cell insulation to reduce standby losses.

3. Distribution and Controls  
   • Optimized Pipework  
     – Minimize pipe lengths and diameters to reduce heat losses and the volume of water in circulation loops.  
     – Design a decentralized loop (e.g., one loop per stairwell) to avoid long runs from a single central plant.  
   • Circulation Loop Controls  
     – Install demand‐controlled circulation pumps that only run when there’s hot‐water draw or user demand, rather than continuous operation.  
     – Fit temperature sensors and timer or sensor‐based on/off control to avoid unnecessary pump runtimes.  
   • Thermostatic Mixing Valves (TMVs)  
     – Position TMVs close to points of use to maintain a constant outlet temperature (e.g., 50 °C) while keeping storage at higher temperatures (e.g., 60–65 °C) to limit legionella growth.

4. System Monitoring and Maintenance  
   • Metering and Submetering  
     – Install water and heat meters for individual apartments or staircases to identify high‐consumption units and encourage conservation.  
   • Regular Servicing  
     – Flush or descale heat‐exchanger surfaces annually.  
     – Check insulation integrity, pump efficiencies, valve operation and recalibrate thermostats.  

5. User Engagement and Behavioral Measures  
   • Feedback Displays  
     – Provide residents with real‐time or monthly consumption data to promote more efficient hot‐water use.  
   • Peak‐Load Management  
     – Stagger water‐heater start times (e.g., via building management system) to avoid coincident peaks and reduce maximum boiler capacity requirements.

By combining high‐efficiency generation, smart storage and insulation, optimized distribution, and ongoing monitoring, you can typically reduce the building’s DHW energy use by 20–40 % while improving comfort and water‐temperature stability for all residents.

An energy declaration (in Swedish “energideklaration”) is an official report that describes a building’s energy performance, its major energy‐using systems and its overall energy efficiency. In Sweden, it is governed by national regulations (Boverket’s provisions) and must be carried out by an authorized energy inspector.  

Key points about an energy declaration:  
• Purpose  
  – To give building owners, buyers or tenants clear information on how much energy a building consumes under normal use.  
  – To identify opportunities for energy savings and guide renovation or technical upgrades.  
• Required content  
  – Energy performance indicator (kWh/m² Atemp and/or total consumption)  
  – Energy classification (epc_energiklass), graded from A (best) to G (worst)  
  – Description of the building’s heated floor area (Atemp), number of floors and stairwells (epc_egenatemp, epc_egenantalplan, epc_egenantaltrapphus)  
  – Main heating, ventilation and cooling systems, including fuel types and efficiencies  
  – Recommendations for cost‐effective energy improvements (e.g. insulation upgrades, system replacements)  
• Administrative details  
  – Each declaration is linked to the building’s unique identifiers (byggnadsid, 01a_fnr, 50a_uuid, 50a_deso, epc_idadr).  
  – It must be updated every ten years or whenever the building undergoes major renovations that affect energy use.  
  – The report is publicly registered so that prospective buyers or tenants can review it before entering into agreements.  

In summary, an energy declaration provides a standardized, transparent assessment of a building’s energy use and efficiency, helping owners and occupants reduce energy costs and environmental impact.

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any upgrade or modification to a building (or its systems) that reduces the amount of energy required to deliver the same level of comfort, safety or productivity. In practice, this means:

• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Adding or upgrading insulation in walls, roofs and floors  
  – Replacing single-glazed windows with high-performance double or triple glazing  
  – Sealing air leaks around doors, windows and service penetrations  

• HVAC and water-heating improvements  
  – Installing high-efficiency boilers, furnaces or heat pumps  
  – Optimizing or retrofitting ventilation systems with heat-recovery units  
  – Upgrading to condensing or tankless water heaters  

• Lighting and controls  
  – Replacing incandescent or fluorescent lamps with LED fixtures  
  – Installing occupancy sensors, daylight dimming and programmable timers  

• Appliances and equipment  
  – Choosing appliances and office equipment with high energy-efficiency ratings (e.g. Energy Star)  
  – Implementing smart controls to reduce standby losses  

Benefits of energy-efficiency improvements include lower energy bills, reduced greenhouse gas emissions, increased occupant comfort and often improved indoor air quality. In an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC), successful efficiency upgrades typically result in a higher (better) energy class and a lower calculated annual energy use.

In the context of building- and energy-performance registration (for example in an Energy Performance Certificate, EPC), a single property may be divided into one or more “premises” or “units,” each of which has its own use-type and associated energy profile.  Below is an overview of the most common premise types and the key ways in which they influence overall energy consumption:

1. Residential Premises  
   • Single-family houses (detached, semi-detached, row houses)  
   • Multi-family dwellings (apartments, condominium blocks)  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Heating and domestic hot water are the dominant loads.  
     – Typical specific consumption (heating + DHW) is on the order of 100–200 kWh/m²·yr (depending on climate, insulation, ventilation strategy and occupant behaviour).  
     – Internal gains (appliances, occupants) offset some heating demand.  

2. Office and Administration Premises  
   • Private offices, open-plan workspaces  
   • Conference rooms, lobbies, cafeterias  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Higher requirements for lighting, cooling and ventilation (often 200–350 kWh/m²·yr total energy).  
     – Longer operational hours (often 8–18 weekdays) and high plug-load density (computers, servers, printers).  

3. Retail and Service Premises  
   • Shops, malls, showrooms  
   • Restaurants, cafés, hair salons, gyms  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Significant lighting loads and, in many cases, refrigeration or kitchen equipment.  
     – Ventilation and air-conditioning demand can be very high in food service and fitness centres.  
     – Specific consumption varies widely—often 250–500 kWh/m²·yr or more in restaurants and supermarkets.  

4. Industrial and Warehouse Premises  
   • Light manufacturing, workshops  
   • Storage and distribution centres  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Process energy (machines, ovens, compressors) can dominate the total.  
     – Building-related loads (heating, lighting) are often secondary—but large volumes (high ceiling halls) increase ventilation and heating demands.  
     – Very wide range: from 100 kWh/m²·yr in simple cold storage up to several thousand kWh/m²·yr in energy-intensive manufacturing.  

5. Public and Institutional Premises  
   • Schools, universities, day-care centres  
   • Hospitals, health clinics  
   • Libraries, museums, community centres  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Hospitals and laboratories often have 24 h operation, strict temperature/humidity control and process loads—up to 500–800 kWh/m²·yr.  
     – Schools and offices within this group typically behave like standard office buildings but may have extended hours.  

6. Special-Purpose Premises  
   • Sports halls, swimming pools  
   • Data-centres, server rooms  
   • Parking garages, agricultural buildings  
   Impact on energy use:  
     – Pools require continuous dehumidification and water heating—specific consumption often exceeds 500 kWh/m²·yr.  
     – Data-centres combine high cooling loads with constant electrical power draw for servers.  
     – Agricultural buildings can be highly variable depending on livestock, crop drying processes, etc.  

How Premise Mix Affects a Property’s Total Energy Use  
– Aggregation: A mixed-use building (for example, ground-floor retail plus upper-floor apartments) will have to allocate heating, cooling and common‐area energy across each premise type in the EPC.  
– Envelope and Systems: Different premises may share the same façade, ventilation system or heating plant—but internal set-points and ventilation rates often differ.  
– Operating Profiles: Varying opening hours, occupancy levels and equipment use mean that simultaneous peak demands can coincide or stagger, affecting plant sizing and load management.  
– Benchmarking and Indicators: In an EPC or energy-declaration context you normally register each premise under its EPC building-type code (epc_egenbyggnadstyp) and heated floor area (Atemp: epc_egenatemp) to calculate specific energy consumption (kWh/m²·yr) for each use category.  

In practice, accurate energy assessment and improvement planning require  
  1. Identifying each premise’s use-type, area and operating schedule  
  2. Characterising shared systems (heating, cooling, ventilation)  
  3. Apportioning total metered energy to the individual premises  
  4. Comparing specific consumption against relevant benchmarks for that use-type  

By doing so, owners and facility managers can pinpoint which premises are driving high energy use—and target renovations, controls or behaviour-change measures where they will have the greatest impact.

In multi-unit buildings the common-area electricity load is typically made up of the following main categories:

1. General and emergency lighting  
   • Corridors, stairwells and lobbies use wall-mounted or ceiling luminaires, often LED, controlled by time switches or occupancy sensors.  
   • Emergency- and exit-sign lighting is on a dedicated, battery-backed circuit to stay on during power failures.

2. Passenger and service lifts  
   • The lift motor and drive electronics draw power each time the car moves.  
   • Car-interior lighting, fan ventilation and control panels add a small continuous draw even when idle.  
   • Modern elevators may use regenerative drives that feed power back into the building grid on descent.

3. Automatic doors and access systems  
   • Lobby and entrance doors with automatic openers use electricity for motors, control boards and safety sensors.  
   • Access-control readers, badge scanners and electric strikes (magnetic locks) also consume standby power.

4. Ventilation and small fans  
   • In some complexes, corridors and lobbies have extract or supply fans to maintain air quality and pressurization (especially in high-rise stairwells).

5. Security, communications and fire-safety equipment  
   • CCTV cameras, intercoms, door-phone systems, and fire-alarm panels all have low but continuous power requirements.  
   • Fire-alarm and smoke-extraction systems often include electrically driven dampers or fans on a backup supply.

6. Cleaning and maintenance outlets  
   • Wall sockets in service cupboards or stairwells supply vacuum cleaners, floor polishers, lifts-shaft lighting, etc.—these are intermittent but part of the common supply.

Management and metering  
– In larger residential or commercial buildings, common-area circuits are often sub-metered so that the co-op or facility manager can separately track and bill these loads.  
– Use of LEDs, occupancy sensors and energy-efficient lift drives is now widespread to minimise running costs and improve the building’s overall energy performance rating.

Apartment buildings typically combine a range of building-envelope, technical-system and user-behavior measures to improve energy performance. Below is a summary of the most common interventions:

1. Envelope Upgrades  
   • Wall insulation: adding internal or external insulation to cavity or solid walls.  
   • Roof and attic insulation: improving thermal resistance of flat roofs, pitched roofs and top-floor ceilings.  
   • Basement and slab insulation: insulating ground-floor slabs and basement walls to reduce heat losses.  
   • High-performance windows and doors: installing double- or triple-glazed units with low-emissivity coatings and thermally broken frames.

Together, these measures can boost a building’s EPC (energy performance certificate) class significantly – for example moving from a Class C or D up toward Class A – and typically yield payback periods of 5–15 years depending on local energy prices and available subsidies.

Natural (passive) ventilation—i.e. the use of wind forces and thermal buoyancy through openings, vents or shafts—has several advantages over fully mechanical (fan‐driven) systems:

1. Lower energy consumption and operating cost  
   • No or minimal fan power is required, so electricity use is very low.  
   • Reduced utility bills over the lifetime of the building.  

2. Simplicity of installation and maintenance  
   • Fewer mechanical components (fans, ductwork, motors) mean lower capital cost.  
   • Less frequent servicing; no filters or moving parts to replace.  

3. Resilience and robustness  
   • Continues to work during power outages or equipment failure.  
   • Less prone to breakdowns and complex repairs.  

4. Indoor air quality and occupant comfort  
   • Provides fresh air directly from outdoors, often perceived as more “natural” and pleasant.  
   • Variable airflow (breezes, stack effect) can enhance thermal comfort if properly designed.  

5. Reduced noise and vibration  
   • No mechanical fans or ducts generating hum or rattles.  
   • Quieter overall indoor environment.  

6. Environmental footprint  
   • Lower embodied energy and carbon footprint over time.  
   • Supports sustainable design objectives when combined with daylighting and passive cooling strategies.  

That said, natural ventilation must be carefully designed to ensure adequate air changes under all weather conditions, and it offers less precise control of temperature and humidity than a mechanical system.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a home is largely a matter of smart design, strategic operation of openings and careful consideration of the local climate. Even without mechanical systems, you can achieve good indoor air quality and thermal comfort by addressing the following points:

1. Building orientation and layout  
   • Place primary living spaces (living room, bedrooms) on sides of the house that receive prevailing breezes.  
   • Arrange rooms so that “clean air” zones (bedrooms, living rooms) are upwind of “pollution-producing” or humid rooms (kitchen, bathroom).  
   • Use open plans or interior partitions with high-level vents to allow air to flow through corridors and common areas.

2. Window and vent placement  
   • Provide operable windows on opposite facades to establish cross-ventilation. Even narrow, staggered openings can induce a strong breeze.  
   • Include high-level vents or clerestory windows to tap into stack effect (warm air rising and exhausting at roof level drives inflow at lower levels).  
   • Install trickle vents in window frames or wall vents in habitable rooms to ensure a minimum continuous airflow, even when windows are closed.

3. Stack-effect design  
   • Incorporate roof-mounted vents or a small chimney-style “thermal shaft.” As indoor air warms, it rises and exits through the top, drawing cooler air in at floor level.  
   • Use internal atria or light-wells fitted with controlled openings at top and bottom to boost vertical airflow.

4. Shading and thermal mass  
   • Provide external shading (eaves, pergolas, shutters) so that solar heat gain is minimized; cooler indoor temperatures help maintain a stronger temperature differential for stack ventilation.  
   • Expose thermal-mass materials (concrete, brick, tile) to daytime breezes; they store coolness and release it at night, stabilizing indoor temperatures.

5. Operable elements and controls  
   • Use windows with multi-stage opening positions (e.g. tilt and turn) so occupants can adjust flow based on wind strength and privacy needs.  
   • Consider automated wind/smoke sensors linked to motorized vents or windows—this keeps airflow optimal when nobody’s on site.  
   • Install screened vents to prevent insects from entering while windows are open.

6. Landscaping and site features  
   • Plant deciduous trees or install trellised vines on windward sides to pre-cool incoming air via evapotranspiration.  
   • Avoid solid fences directly upwind; instead use permeable hedges that break the wind just enough to reduce turbulence without blocking airflow completely.

7. Maintenance and commissioning  
   • Keep vents and window tracks clean and unobstructed.  
   • Perform “smoke‐test” walkthroughs: use incense or a small smoke machine to visualize airflow patterns and identify dead zones.  
   • Adjust furniture layouts and internal doors to eliminate stagnant corners.

By combining these strategies—cross-ventilation, stack effect, well‐placed operable openings, shading, and smart landscape design—you can greatly improve air exchange rates and occupant comfort without relying on mechanical systems.

When you’re evaluating whether to install solar panels on a property, it pays to look at several technical, financial and regulatory factors up front.  Below is a checklist of the most important considerations:

1. Roof and Site Suitability  
   • Orientation and Tilt – South-facing roofs with a pitch of 30–40° typically generate the most energy in northern Europe. East- or west-facing roofs also work, but output will be lower.  
   • Shading – Even partial shading from trees, chimneys or neighboring buildings can reduce panel output significantly. A shade analysis (on-site or with smartphone apps) is essential.  
   • Roof Condition and Structure – Panels last 25 years or more, so roofs and supporting rafters should be in good condition. Factor in the cost of any roof repairs or reinforcement before installation.  
   • Available Surface Area – Measure how many panels will physically fit. An average 1 kW of panels needs about 6–8 m².

2. System Size and Equipment  
   • Panel Type and Efficiency – Monocrystalline panels are more efficient (15–22 %) but more expensive. Polycrystalline are cheaper but less efficient.  
   • Inverter Selection – String inverters are common and cost-effective. Micro-inverters on each panel boost performance under partial shading but cost more.  
   • Mounting System – Roof hooks, ballast mounts or building-integrated systems. Choose corrosion-resistant materials and ensure proper waterproofing.

3. Energy Production and Usage  
   • Load Profile – Review your annual electricity consumption. An EPC (energy performance certificate) can give you your building’s total annual use and help size the array.  
   • Self-Consumption vs. Export – Maximize on‐site consumption to improve payback. Inverters with export controls or battery storage can help absorb surplus production.

4. Financial Analysis  
   • Up-Front Costs – Panels, inverter, mounting, installation labour, permits and grid‐connection fees.  
   • Incentives and Subsidies – Research local or national grants, tax credits, feed-in tariffs or green-loan programmes that can reduce capital outlay.  
   • Electricity Prices and Tariffs – The higher your retail electricity cost, the faster your solar investment repays itself. Also check the export tariff if you plan to sell surplus energy back to the grid.  
   • Payback Period and ROI – Calculate expected annual generation × avoided grid cost, minus any fixed charges (grid fees, meter rental). Typical payback in Sweden is 7–12 years, depending on incentives and system size.  

5. Legal and Regulatory Requirements  
   • Building Permits and Declarations – In many municipalities you must notify or apply for a permit (bygglov) before mounting panels, especially on heritage or protected buildings.  
   • Grid Connection Agreement – Sign a contract with your Distribution System Operator (DSO). They will install a bidirectional meter and set export limits if needed.

6. Operation, Maintenance and Monitoring  
   • Cleaning and Inspection – Panels are low‐maintenance but benefit from an annual wash (rain and dirt can reduce output by up to 5–10 %).  
   • Performance Monitoring – Install a monitoring system (inverter-integrated or third-party) to track output, detect faults and verify warranty claims.  
   • Warranties and Service Contracts – Look for a minimum 10–12 year product warranty on panels, 5–10 years on inverters, plus optional maintenance agreements.

7. Future Proofing  
   • Battery Storage – Adding batteries boosts self‐consumption and adds resilience during grid outages—but increases capital cost.  
   • System Expansion – Check that your inverter and roof space can accommodate future panel additions if your energy needs grow.  
   • Technology Trends – Keep an eye on rapidly improving panel efficiency, battery chemistries and smart-home integration.

By systematically evaluating these points—site potential, system design, financial returns and regulatory steps—you’ll be able to size a solar installation that best matches your roof, your energy use and your budget. This preparation will help ensure a smooth permitting process, reliable performance and the strongest possible return on your investment.

Energy classes (often shown on the familiar A – G or A+++ – D scale) are designed to help you compare how much electricity or fuel an appliance will use in normal operation. From an energy-perspective, choosing higher-rated appliances has the following advantages:

1. Lower operating costs  
   • An A + + + refrigerator typically uses 30–50 % less electricity than a C-rated model of the same size.  
   • Over the appliance’s lifetime, these savings often offset any small price premium up-front.  

2. Reduced environmental impact  
   • Less energy consumption means fewer CO₂ emissions (assuming you’re on a grid powered by fossil fuels).  
   • In countries moving towards renewable electricity, high-class appliances help you benefit more quickly from a cleaner mix.  

3. Better match to a building’s overall energy performance  
   • In a building with a high EPC energy class (e.g. A or B), heat losses and ventilation needs are minimized. Installing A-class appliances ensures that your remaining energy use (fridges, washers, ovens) is as efficient as possible, further lowering total energy demand.  
   • Conversely, in an older or poorly insulated building (E – G class), every kilowatt saved on appliances directly reduces the load on already strained heating or cooling systems.  

4. Long-term value and incentives  
   • Many utility- or government-run schemes offer rebates or tax deductions for purchasing top-rated appliances.  
   • Resale value of a property can improve if it is equipped with modern, energy-efficient equipment.  

How to use labels in practice  
  • Always compare models of the same capacity or performance class when looking at their energy labels.  
  • Look at the annual energy consumption figure (kWh/year or kWh/100 cycles).  
  • Consider additional features such as eco-programs, inverter compressors or sensors—these often boost real-world efficiency beyond the class alone.  

In summary, selecting appliances with the highest available energy class is one of the simplest and most cost-effective ways to reduce both your energy bills and your carbon footprint, while complementing the energy performance of your building as expressed by its EPC energy class.

When shopping for a refrigerator or freezer with low energy consumption, consider the following features and specifications:

1. Energy Efficiency Class  
   • Look for the highest possible rating on your region’s labeling scheme (e.g. EU A-G scale or ENERGY STAR®).  
   • The more efficient the class (A+++, A++ or ENERGY STAR®), the lower your electricity bill over the appliance’s lifetime.

   • A variable-speed (inverter) compressor adjusts cooling power to suit demand, rather than running at full speed all the time.  
   • This reduces peaks in power draw, cuts noise levels and improves long-term reliability.

3. Size and Capacity Appropriate to Your Needs  
   • Choosing a refrigerator or freezer that closely matches your household’s storage needs prevents wasted energy cooling unused space.  
   • Models with flexible shelving or convertible compartments let you optimize size (e.g. converting a freezer section into extra fridge space).

4. Advanced Insulation and Door Seals  
   • High-performance insulation (often thicker polyurethane foam) slows heat gain and reduces how often the compressor runs.  
   • Magnetic door gaskets that seal tightly prevent cold air from escaping—check that seals close firmly and have no gaps.

5. Frost-Free or No-Frost Function  
   • Automatic defrost cycles prevent ice buildup, maintaining airflow and efficient heat exchange inside the freezer.  
   • Although the defrost heater uses extra energy intermittently, modern frost-free designs are generally more efficient than manual-defrost units over time.

6. LED Interior Lighting  
   • LED lights use up to 75% less electricity than incandescent bulbs and produce less heat, reducing the workload on the compressor.

7. Smart or Adaptive Controls  
   • Digital thermostats with precise temperature regulation avoid overcooling.  
   • Some models include “eco” modes, vacation settings or sensors that detect ambient room temperature and adjust cooling accordingly.

8. Separate Cooling Circuits or Drawers  
   • Models with distinct cooling systems for fridge and freezer compartments prevent cold-air mixing—this maintains each compartment at its optimal temperature with less overall energy use.

9. Heat-Rejection Design and Placement  
   • Look for a model with good ventilation at the back or sides.  
   • When installing, leave adequate clearance around the appliance so heat can dissipate easily; this helps the compressor run less often.

10. Additional Features That Promote Efficiency  
   • Door-open alarms remind you to close the door quickly.  
   • Air-filtration or anti-bacterial systems may keep food fresher longer, reducing the frequency of temperature fluctuations caused by opening and closing the door.

By combining a top-tier energy-efficiency rating with inverter technology, good insulation, frost-free operation and smart temperature controls, you’ll minimize the fridge/freezer’s electricity consumption and operating cost over its lifetime.

In Sweden (and in many other deregulated electricity markets) you always need two separate agreements to have power in your home or business:

1. Grid contract (nätavtal)  
   • Who you sign with: the local network operator (the company that owns and maintains the power lines and transformers in your area).  
   • What it covers:  
     – Physical delivery of electricity from the transmission grid out to your property.  
     – Operation, maintenance and development of the local distribution network.  
     – Meter reading, network capacity reservation and related services (e.g. remote reading, fault notifications).  
   • How you pay: typically a fixed monthly or annual fee plus a variable charge based on how much current (kW) you’re allowed to draw, and/or how much energy (kWh) you consume according to the meter.  
   • Your responsibility: ensure safe access for network operator staff; report any outages or meter faults.

2. Electricity supply contract (elhandelsavtal)  
   • Who you sign with: an electricity supplier or retailer (this can be the same company as your network operator, but it doesn’t have to be).  
   • What it covers:  
     – Purchase of the electrical energy (kWh) you actually consume.  
     – Choice of pricing model: spot-price pass-through (monthly or hourly Nord Pool prices), fixed price, block tariff, green product (renewable certificates), etc.  
     – Invoicing, customer service, optional value-added services (carbon offsets, automated price switching, billing alerts).  
   • How you pay: based on the chosen tariff – e.g. hourly spot price + margin, fixed wholesale price, or other bundled offers. May include a small supplier fee.  
   • Your responsibility: monitoring your consumption, choosing a suitable contract type, and switching supplier when it makes sense.

Key takeaway:  
• The grid contract ensures the wires and infrastructure that bring power to your property are maintained and available.  
• The electricity supply contract governs the actual sale and pricing of the energy you use.  

Even if you get both services from the same corporate group, they remain legally and operationally separate. Always check and compare both your network fees and your electricity tariff to optimize your total cost.

Control and regulation technology (often called building automation or process control) refers to the hardware and software systems used to monitor, manage and automatically adjust a building’s technical installations—primarily heating, ventilation, air-conditioning, lighting, shading, and sometimes security or fire‐safety systems. Its main purpose is to

1. Maintain occupant comfort  
   – Keep temperatures, humidity and air quality within specified ranges  
   – Ensure consistent lighting levels and appropriate air flow  

2. Optimize energy use  
   – Switch equipment on or off (or modulate power) based on real-time needs  
   – Implement schedules, setback periods and demand-response strategies  

3. Improve operational reliability and safety  
   – Detect equipment faults or unsafe conditions (e.g. overpressure, smoke)  
   – Trigger alarms or emergency shutdowns if thresholds are exceeded  

Key components of control and regulation technology include:  
• Sensors (temperature, humidity, CO₂, light level, pressure, etc.)  
• Controllers / programmable logic controllers (PLCs) or dedicated building-management computers  
• Actuators (valves, dampers, variable-speed drives, relays)  
• Communication networks / buses (e.g. BACnet, Modbus, KNX)  
• User interfaces and visualization tools (touch panels, SCADA, web dashboards)  

By integrating these elements, a control-and-regulation system continuously reads building conditions, compares them to target set-points, and issues commands so that pumps, fans, boilers, chillers, lighting circuits and other devices operate in the most efficient, comfortable and safe way.

Expanding a building‐automation or process‐control system is fundamentally about choosing a modular, open‐architecture approach up front and then adding hardware, software and network elements in a controlled way. Even without specific context, the following general steps and best practices apply:

1. Define the Expansion Requirements  
   • Identify new functions (e.g., additional temperature zones, lighting scenes, security points).  
   • Quantify required I/O points (analog inputs, digital inputs/outputs, relays, actuators).  
   • Establish performance targets (scan times, response times, data-logging rates).  

2. Verify Existing Architecture and Compatibility  
   • Check that your current controller/PLC supports additional I/O modules or “slaves.”  
   • Confirm that bus protocols in use (BACnet, Modbus, KNX, LonWorks, etc.) allow additional nodes.  
   • Review power, cabinet space and cooling margins to handle extra modules.  

3. Select and Install Hardware Modules  
   • Choose compatible I/O cards, communication gateways or field controllers from the same vendor family (or open‐protocol third parties).  
   • Mount new modules on the DIN rail, rack or directly on local substations as appropriate.  
   • Wire sensors, valves, switches, actuators or other field devices to the new I/O terminals.  

4. Update Network and Communication Layer  
   • Address or subnet any new controllers or I/O devices so they don’t conflict with existing nodes.  
   • If you exceed bus-segment length or node count, install repeaters or routers to maintain signal integrity.  
   • Verify data‐security and authentication settings if you are adding IP-based devices.  

5. Extend the Control Logic  
   • Using your programming environment (e.g., ladder, function block, structured text), integrate new inputs and outputs into the existing control strategy.  
   • Encapsulate new sequences or interlocks in modular program blocks for ease of troubleshooting and future growth.  
   • Document all new variables, addresses and interdependencies.  

6. Update Supervisory/Visualization Software  
   • Add new points to your SCADA or building‐management HMI. Group them logically (e.g., by floor or system).  
   • Configure any new trends, alarms, schedules or reporting functions.  
   • Test alarm thresholds and notifications for the added equipment.  

7. Commissioning and Validation  
   • Perform point-to-point checks: verify that each physical input/output behaves correctly in the control logic.  
   • Run end‐to‐end functional tests under normal and failure conditions (e.g., sensor fault, communication loss).  
   • Record commissioning data and update the system manuals.  

8. Training and Maintenance  
   • Train operations and maintenance staff on the new equipment and revised software screens.  
   • Update maintenance schedules (e.g., calibration intervals for added sensors).  
   • Incorporate the changes into your change‐management and spare-parts inventory processes.  

By following these steps—starting from clear requirements, using a modular architecture, ensuring network and protocol compatibility, and carrying out systematic testing—you can expand virtually any control system in a robust, scalable way.

In practice the divide between “normal” (sometimes called slow or destination) charging and “fast” charging is based on power level and charging technology. Although definitions vary slightly by region and standard, a common breakdown is:  

1. AC (alternating‐current) charging – uses the vehicle’s onboard charger  
   • Slow or “trickle” charging: up to ~3.7 kW (single‐phase, 16 A at 230 V)  
   • Normal charging: 3.7 – 11 kW (single‐phase up to 32 A or three‐phase at 16 A)  
   • Fast AC charging: 11 – 22 kW (three‐phase, 32 A per phase)  
   Note: Some markets and standards (e.g. IEC Mode 3) allow up to 43 kW AC, but in most public installations you will see 22 kW as the upper limit for “fast” AC.  

2. DC (direct‐current) fast charging – bypasses the onboard charger and feeds power directly to the battery  
   • DC fast charging: typically starts at 25–50 kW and goes up to 150 kW  
   • Ultra-fast or rapid charging: 150 – 350 kW (and beyond in some ultra-rapid stations)  

Key boundary points:  
– If you stay on AC and under about 22 kW, you’re in the “normal” to “AC fast” charging realm, using the vehicle’s onboard electronics.  
– Once you move above ~22 kW AC (and especially when you switch to a DC supply of 25 – 50 kW or higher), you’re firmly in the “fast” or “rapid” charging category.  

In summary, most practitioners treat AC charging up to 22 kW as normal/fast AC charging, and DC charging from roughly 25–50 kW upwards as true fast (or rapid) charging.

Load balancing for electric-vehicle (EV) charging is the method by which available electrical power is distributed intelligently among one or more charging points to

• Prevent overloads on a building’s electrical installation or on the local grid  
• Maximize utilization of the available capacity  
• Ensure each vehicle receives a fair or prioritized share of power  

How it works  
1. Capacity monitoring  
  – A central controller or smart meter continuously measures total current draw and compares it with the maximum allowable capacity of the service connection or sub-feed.  
2. Power allocation  
  – If multiple EVs plug in simultaneously, the controller dynamically adjusts the charging current to each point so that the sum does not exceed the predefined limit.  
  – Charging currents can be reduced or increased in real time as vehicles start, finish or change their charging rate.  
3. Priority settings (optional)  
  – Some systems allow you to assign priorities—for example, a company fleet vehicle may be given higher charging priority than a visitor’s car.  
4. Integration with building energy management  
  – Load-balancing controllers can be tied into the building’s energy-management system or to on-site renewable sources (solar, battery storage) to further optimize costs and self-consumption.  

Types of load balancing  
• Static load balancing  
  – Power limits are set in advance for each charger. Distribution does not adjust in real time—when one charger reaches its limit, others pick up the slack.  
• Dynamic load balancing  
  – Real-time measurement and adjustment. The most common approach in modern EV-charging installations.  

Key benefits  
• Safety—avoids tripping breakers or fuses by keeping total draw within safe limits  
• Cost efficiency—allows more chargers to be installed on a given supply without costly grid upgrades  
• User experience—minimizes “no-charge” situations and reduces waiting times by sharing power fairly  
• Grid friendliness—smooths out peaks in demand, which can reduce energy costs and stress on the local distribution network  

In summary, load balancing is a crucial feature in any multi-point EV charging installation, ensuring reliable, efficient and safe distribution of electrical power.

Improving lighting in basement areas requires a combination of maximizing available natural light (where possible), specifying the right types of fixtures and controls, and designing for both functionality and comfort. Below are several strategies you can consider:

1. Maximize Natural Light  
  • Light wells and window wells – If your basement is partially below grade, install or enlarge window wells with reflective interior surfaces to bring in more daylight.  
  • Glass block windows – Provide daylight while maintaining privacy and moisture protection.  
  • Sun tunnels (tubular daylighting devices) – Capture roof or higher-level daylight and channel it down through reflective tubes into the basement.

2. Layer Your Artificial Lighting  
  a. Ambient lighting  
    – Recessed LED downlights with wide beam angles for even, general illumination.  
    – Surface-mounted or semi-flush ceiling fixtures if ceiling height is limited.  
  b. Task lighting  
    – Under-cabinet or under-shelf LED strips for workbenches, laundry areas or reading nooks.  
    – Adjustable wall-mounted swing-arm lamps for hobby or desk spaces.  
  c. Accent lighting  
    – LED wall washers or uplights to highlight architectural features, artwork or storage alcoves.  
    – Cove lighting along perimeter walls to increase the sense of height and openness.

3. Choose Appropriate Fixtures and Lamps  
  • LED technology – Opt for high efficacy (lumens per watt), long-life LEDs with good color rendering index (CRI ≥ 80) to ensure colors look natural.  
  • Color temperature – A neutral-to-warm white (3000–3500 K) is typically most comfortable in living or recreation areas; cooler whites (4000 K) can work in utility or workshop spaces.  
  • Moisture and dust protection – For basements prone to dampness, select fixtures with an appropriate IP rating (e.g. IP44 or higher) to guard against splashes and condensation.

4. Control and Zoning  
  • Multi-circuit zoning – Divide the basement into lighting zones (storage, laundry, lounge, corridor) so you only power the areas in use.  
  • Dimmers and scene controls – Add dimmer switches or smart lighting controls (e.g. DALI, Zigbee) to adjust light levels for different activities.  
  • Occupancy sensors – PIR or microwave sensors can automatically switch lights on/off in less-frequently used areas such as corridors, storage rooms or bathrooms.

5. Reflective and Architectural Enhancements  
  • Light-colored walls and ceilings – Painting surfaces white or light pastel increases light reflectance and helps distribute illumination.  
  • Gloss or satin finishes – These finishes can subtly bounce light around the room without creating glare.  
  • Mirrors and glass accents – Strategically placed mirrors can amplify both natural and artificial light sources.

6. Ensure Proper Light Levels  
  – General living spaces: 200–300 lux  
  – Task areas (desks, workbenches): 300–500 lux  
  – Storage corridors: 100–200 lux  
  Use a light meter or consult an electrician/lighting designer to verify you meet recommended levels.

7. Safety and Code Considerations  
  • Emergency and egress lighting – If the basement is occupied or used as a rental unit, local building codes may require emergency exit lighting or illuminated exit signs.  
  • Wiring and circuits – All basement lighting should comply with national and local electrical codes, including GFCI protection where required.

By combining daylight-enhancing measures with a well-zoned, layered LED lighting scheme and smart controls, you’ll create a bright, comfortable and energy-efficient basement environment.

Here are several proven strategies for reducing energy use for domestic hot water (DHW) in an apartment building:

1. Improve Distribution Efficiency  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes, storage tanks and heat exchangers to minimize standby losses.  
   • Install properly sized, demand-controlled recirculation pumps with timers or temperature sensors so water only circulates when needed.

2. Recover Waste Heat  
   • Fit a drain-water heat recovery unit (plate heat exchanger) that captures heat from showers and drains to pre-heat incoming cold water.  
   • Consider heat recovery ventilation (HRV/ERV) systems that transfer heat from exhaust air to the DHW loop.

3. Upgrade the Heat Source  
   • Replace old boilers or electric heaters with high-efficiency condensing boilers (COP > 0.90) or dedicated DHW heat pumps (COP 2.5–4).  
   • Where climate and roof orientation allow, add solar thermal collectors or photovoltaic-driven heat-pump pre-heating to offset peak loads.

4. Optimize Temperature Set-Points  
   • Lower the storage tank temperature to the minimum safe level (typically 55–60 °C) and use thermostatic mixing valves at points of use to prevent scalding.  
   • Balance water temperatures so you’re neither overheating nor underheating—each degree you reduce can save roughly 2–3 % of DHW energy.

5. Reduce Water Consumption  
   • Install low-flow showerheads, faucet aerators, and efficient sanitary fittings to cut water—and thus heating—demand by 20–50 %.  
   • Encourage residents to shorten showers and fix drips promptly to avoid unnecessary hot-water use.

6. Metering and User Feedback  
   • Sub-meter DHW consumption per apartment and provide residents with real-time feedback or billing by usage. This encourages conservation behavior.  
   • Share monthly or quarterly consumption reports and tips for further savings.

   • Flush and descale tanks, heat exchangers, and showerheads periodically to maintain heat-transfer efficiency.  
   • Check and calibrate thermostats, mixing valves, pumps and controls at least once a year.

By combining insulation and distribution improvements with high-efficiency heating equipment, waste‐heat recovery, water‐saving fittings and active resident engagement, an apartment building can typically cut DHW energy use by 30–60 %—lowering both operating costs and carbon footprint.

Ventilation balancing refers to the commissioning process by which a building’s mechanical ventilation system is adjusted so that each supply and exhaust fan delivers exactly the design-specified airflow rate in each zone or room. Properly balanced ventilation is fundamental to both indoor comfort and energy efficiency. Here’s why it matters for energy use:

1. Minimizes heat losses and gains  
   • If you supply more outdoor air than you exhaust (or vice versa), the building envelope will experience unwanted pressure differences. That drives uncontrolled infiltration or exfiltration of air through cracks and gaps, increasing heat losses in winter and heat gains in summer.  
   • A balanced system, especially one equipped with heat‐recovery (HRV/ERV), recovers a large portion of the thermal energy in the exhaust air and transfers it to the incoming air stream. This can cut heating or cooling loads by up to 60–80 %.

2. Reduces fan and pump energy  
   • Fans that are under‐ or over-sized relative to actual ductwork resistance will draw more electrical power than necessary. During balancing, fan speeds (or inlet vanes) are set so that each branch of the duct network sees the correct static pressure and flow.  
   • This matching of fan output to system resistance typically reduces fan energy consumption by 10–30 %.

3. Ensures compliance with design ventilation rates  
   • Over-ventilation wastes energy by conditioning (heating/cooling) more outdoor air than needed for air quality.  
   • Under-ventilation compromises IAQ and may lead occupants to open windows, causing further uncontrolled losses. A balanced system delivers exactly the fresh-air flow that was specified in the design, no more, no less.

4. Improves overall system performance  
   • Balanced airflow helps maintain correct indoor pressures, protecting against moisture problems (mould risk) and ensuring that air actually passes through the intended filters and heat exchangers.  
   • Well-commissioned systems run more quietly and require less frequent service calls, reducing both operating costs and downtime.

In summary, ventilation balancing is the fine-tuning of your mechanical air‐handling system so that it runs exactly as intended. By doing so, you avoid wasting fan power, prevent unnecessary heating and cooling losses, and ensure that any heat-recovery devices operate at their rated efficiency—delivering better comfort at lower energy cost.

   • Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – if the building currently relies on natural or extract-only ventilation, an MVHR system can recover up to 80 % of the outgoing heat.  
   • Air tightness – a blower-door test will show if draught-proofing is needed around windows, doors and service penetrations.

4. Renewable energy integration  
   • Solar photovoltaic (PV) panels – if the roof orientation and structure allow, PV can offset electricity use.  
   • Solar thermal or heat pumps – for domestic hot water, solar thermal collectors or a dedicated hot-water heat pump can cut heating bills further.
